The growth idea: money grows by earning returns over time

The honest framing: future value is a projection, not a promise; rates change

The future value interest factor (1 + r)^n and how it grows with time and rate
Annual compounding as the default assumption in the lesson
Interest rate defined as earned by the lender and charged to the borrower

claims.claim: Future value (FV) is the amount a specific sum of money today will be worth at a future point in time when it earns interest or returns; OpenStax Principles of Finance states that future value refers to how a specific amount of money today can have greater value tomorrow.
Money held in interest-bearing accounts or investments grows over time as interest income accrues or returns are realized on the investment — the growth idea behind future value.

The future value of a single amount is computed as FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, where PV is the present value or starting amount, r is the interest (growth) rate per period, and n is the number of periods; the (1 + r)^n portion is the future value interest factor, which rises as either r or n increases.

With annual compounding, each year's interest is earned on the full running balance, so interest from earlier periods earns its own interest in later periods (interest on interest), which makes the balance grow in accelerating increments the longer the money stays invested.

Future value and present value are the same time-value relationship read in opposite directions: compounding carries today's money forward to a future value, while discounting brings a future amount back to its present value; OpenStax describes discounting as the exact opposite of compounding.

Future value thinking supports personal financial goals — for example checking whether a starting deposit at a stated rate reaches a savings target — and the SEC's Investor.gov provides a compound interest calculator so savers can project how money grows toward a goal over time.

A future-value figure depends directly on the interest rate assumed and the number of periods considered; because the rate is an assumption that can change, a calculated future value is a projection under stated assumptions rather than a guarantee of the amount that will actually be received.

The interest rate concept applies to borrowing as well as saving: the rate is earned by the original lender of funds and charged to the borrower, so the amount a borrower owes grows over time by the same future-value mathematics.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which symbol and name to use for the rate in the future-value formula.
positions: r, called the interest rate and also the growth rate (OpenStax Principles of Finance)
i, called the interest rate or other return that can be earned on the money (CFI)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses r and describes it as the annual rate of return (interest earned or growth applied), so the concept transfers across the two notations.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a computed future value is a prediction about the future.
positions: It is a deterministic calculation: given inputs, the output is exact (both sources)
The realized amount is uncertain because the assumed rate may not hold over time (OpenStax's dependence of FV on r and n)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both halves honestly: the arithmetic is exact, while the outcome is a projection built on an assumed rate — the honest framing section states this explicitly.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How compounding frequency affects the result.
positions: Annual compounding assumed in the simple single-amount formula (OpenStax 7.2, CFI example)
More frequent compounding changes the future value (OpenStax 7.4 lists compounding-period frequency as a topic of its own)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson assumes annual compounding throughout, notes the assumption, and leaves compounding frequency to the compound-interest sibling topic.
